body: Both are described by ISTP as the same set of preferences, which is the premise of a same-type comparison: attention and energy lean inward, information is gathered with weight on facts and first-hand experience, judgement leans on objective consistent standards, and the outer world tends toward keeping options rather than settling at once. With the same four letters, the behavioural common ground is far larger than the difference.

In 16Personalities' NERIS Identity scale, Assertive describes steadier self-assurance. Turbulent describes greater sensitivity to pressure and a stronger tendency to second-guess yourself. Both people can reach the same assessment of a fault and feel differently about their own work.

In a fictional repair, the same sealing machine returns after servicing. Two technicians can look at the same work order and check the same readings. Afterward, one might still feel confident in the initial assessment while the other wonders whether it missed something. Neither their confidence nor their actions determine whether the machine meets the release requirements.

Actions do not separate the ends. Someone retests on the spot, someone first asks the customer what consumable was changed, and either can appear at either end. What can be reviewed is the self-assessment at that moment: after this diagnosis was overturned, how much confidence remains in your next judgement.

To leave a record that can be looked back on, write down the conclusion, the basis and the confidence at the time; after the recheck write another entry stating which evidence was added, whether the test conditions changed and which way the confidence moved. When the two conclusions disagree, first work out whether more evidence appeared or the conditions changed, and do not infer the emotion at the time from the size of the gap between the two columns.

A recurring experience can help in understanding a test result, but a work order record cannot decide A or T. Whether once or many times, the retesting action and the feeling at the time are not rules for deciding a suffix. The four letters and the function order are on the [ISTP base page](/en/personality/istp), and the definitions of the two terms are in the [NERIS account](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory).

The notation used here is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe for ISTP. The third process is Intuition, written as Ni in this convention. The Myers & Briggs Foundation also lists Ne for that position. Fe is the fourth process. A/T does not change this theoretical order or tell you what someone will do first.

body: One work order offers five things worth looking at: whether you trust yourself when writing the conclusion, how much confidence in your judgement remains after being contradicted on the spot, how much assurance is left when downtime presses, how you assess your own ability, and how you assess this judgement after the machine goes back.

There is no question of who is more accurate or faster in the table, only of self-assessment. Align three things before reading: whether the same sentence was heard, whether the same responsibility is carried, and whether it is the same work order in hand. A person carrying heavier responsibility naturally feels it more strongly, and it may simply be a different post. In every row the external basis is fixed to the same readings, the same recheck and the same acceptance standard, and all that either end may attend to more is the movement of its own confidence.
The five rows below are five angles chosen by the editors, using one fictional sealing-machine rework to illustrate the two ends of the same Identity dimension:

| The angle observed | ISTP-A (Assertive) | ISTP-T (Turbulent) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Confidence when writing the diagnosis | More inclined to trust that "this inference holds", while still rechecking the same readings | More inclined to suspect "an item was missed", while rechecking the same readings |
| When contradicted on the spot | Hearing the same objection, may still be confident about the other grounds for the inference | Hearing the same objection, may doubt more whether the whole inference holds |
| When downtime presses | May still feel confident in the assessment under time pressure; release depends on the required readings | May feel less certain about the assessment under the same time pressure; release depends on the same readings |
| After finding the same missed point | May see the omission as a specific error and remain confident in their skills | May worry the same error reflects a wider gap in their skills |
| After the machine is returned to the customer | After meeting the same release criteria, may still feel confident about the original assessment | After meeting the same release criteria, may feel less sure of the original assessment |

If an objection raises a safety issue, the same required checks apply regardless of the suffix or how the technician feels. A sharp tone can affect either person. New evidence may give either person a reason to revise their assessment.

body: Neither reading holds: A does not mean being unable to take advice, and T does not mean being bad at the trade. These two words mark where self-assessment lands, not a score for skill in hand, and they do not measure the quality of a judgement.

To compare who is steadier, do not compare who talks less. Go back to the work order: the original readings, the replacement record, the time of the customer's answer. Who measured what is in the record; that is closer to the facts than who looks more composed.

Another slip is writing the right-hand letter into the code as a fifth letter and reading it as another type. The second letter of ISTP is still S and the third still T; A and T are two ends of one dimension in NERIS Identity, they sit alongside those four rather than composing them, and they are not an official MBTI dimension.

One rework or one retest is not enough to decide a suffix by itself; conversely, a recurring reaction cannot become a decision rule either. On the same work order, either end may retest and either may ask a colleague to check. To compare two results, see the note on retesting in the questions below.

body: This section does not decide which end you belong to; it only says in which situation one description is closer to your reaction at the time. When the two results are uncertain, do not fight over the label: go back to the work order and write the original judgement and the recheck result in two columns.

When a troubleshooting conclusion is contradicted, note first whether it can be checked against the same readings or records, then record separately whether assurance in the original explanation changed. With different equipment, heavier responsibility or a tighter deadline, the experience may differ. Either end can recheck to the process, and this record cannot decide a suffix either.

How to write the two columns: the left records the conclusion, the basis and the confidence at the time; the right records the readings after the recheck, the new evidence, the change in conditions and the change in confidence. Whether or not the conclusions agree, keep the two columns separate; the size of the difference only shows that the judgement then and the material later were different, not the strength of an emotion, and it does not decide how you should assess yourself.

This record is only for reviewing the self-assessment at the time, not for judging who is better suited to repair work. Whether once or many times, the retesting action and the feeling at the time are not rules for deciding a suffix.

body: **Framework sources** The four letters of official MBTI and type dynamics follow the [Foundation's type dynamics table](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/); the explanation of A/T follows the [16Personalities account of NERIS](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory) and the [Identity page](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent).

**The type-dynamics convention used here** This page uses Ti–Se–Ni–Fe for ISTP. The Foundation's table allows either attitude for the third process, Intuition. Here Ni means introverted intuition in position three, and Fe means extraverted feeling in position four. The suffix adds no process and has no bearing on skills or behaviour order.

**Editorial fiction statement** The sealing-machine rework and the work order recheck, the lab report sent back, and the conversation in which a partner mentions the leaking tap are all editorial fiction, used only for practice in telling things apart, and correspond to no real work order, report or person.

**Scope limits** This page uses the NERIS definition of Identity for A/T; that definition is not the scoring method of the FermatMind assessment and provides no evidence for its norms. How FermatMind scores and how results are interpreted are set out in the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence). The four-letter sample distribution of MBTI Form M cannot be used to estimate how many people sit at NERIS A/T. Results have to be read together with the setting in which the questions were answered and recent experience, and are not for hiring screening, relationship prediction or ranking ability; health and safety matters follow professional guidance, with clinical judgement resting on a qualified professional.

body: Both are described by ISTP as the same set of preferences, which is the premise of a same-type comparison: attention and energy lean inward, information is gathered with weight on facts and first-hand experience, judgement leans on objective consistent standards, and the outer world tends toward keeping options rather than settling at once. With the same four letters, the behavioural common ground is far larger than the difference.

In 16Personalities' NERIS Identity scale, Assertive describes steadier self-assurance. Turbulent describes greater sensitivity to pressure and a stronger tendency to second-guess yourself. Both people can reach the same assessment of a fault and feel differently about their own work.

In a fictional repair, the same sealing machine returns after servicing. Two technicians can look at the same work order and check the same readings. Afterward, one might still feel confident in the initial assessment while the other wonders whether it missed something. Neither their confidence nor their actions determine whether the machine meets the release requirements.

Actions do not separate the ends. Someone retests on the spot, someone first asks the customer what consumable was changed, and either can appear at either end. What can be reviewed is the self-assessment at that moment: after this diagnosis was overturned, how much confidence remains in your next judgement.

To leave a record that can be looked back on, write down the conclusion, the basis and the confidence at the time; after the recheck write another entry stating which evidence was added, whether the test conditions changed and which way the confidence moved. When the two conclusions disagree, first work out whether more evidence appeared or the conditions changed, and do not infer the emotion at the time from the size of the gap between the two columns.

A recurring experience can help in understanding a test result, but a work order record cannot decide A or T. Whether once or many times, the retesting action and the feeling at the time are not rules for deciding a suffix. The four letters and the function order are on the [ISTP base page](/en/personality/istp), and the definitions of the two terms are in the [NERIS account](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory).

The notation used here is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe for ISTP. The third process is Intuition, written as Ni in this convention. The Myers & Briggs Foundation also lists Ne for that position. Fe is the fourth process. A/T does not change this theoretical order or tell you what someone will do first.

body: One work order offers five things worth looking at: whether you trust yourself when writing the conclusion, how much confidence in your judgement remains after being contradicted on the spot, how much assurance is left when downtime presses, how you assess your own ability, and how you assess this judgement after the machine goes back.

There is no question of who is more accurate or faster in the table, only of self-assessment. Align three things before reading: whether the same sentence was heard, whether the same responsibility is carried, and whether it is the same work order in hand. A person carrying heavier responsibility naturally feels it more strongly, and it may simply be a different post. In every row the external basis is fixed to the same readings, the same recheck and the same acceptance standard, and all that either end may attend to more is the movement of its own confidence.
The five rows below are five angles chosen by the editors, using one fictional sealing-machine rework to illustrate the two ends of the same Identity dimension:

| The angle observed | ISTP-A (Assertive) | ISTP-T (Turbulent) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Confidence when writing the diagnosis | More inclined to trust that "this inference holds", while still rechecking the same readings | More inclined to suspect "an item was missed", while rechecking the same readings |
| When contradicted on the spot | Hearing the same objection, may still be confident about the other grounds for the inference | Hearing the same objection, may doubt more whether the whole inference holds |
| When downtime presses | May still feel confident in the assessment under time pressure; release depends on the required readings | May feel less certain about the assessment under the same time pressure; release depends on the same readings |
| After finding the same missed point | May see the omission as a specific error and remain confident in their skills | May worry the same error reflects a wider gap in their skills |
| After the machine is returned to the customer | After meeting the same release criteria, may still feel confident about the original assessment | After meeting the same release criteria, may feel less sure of the original assessment |

If an objection raises a safety issue, the same required checks apply regardless of the suffix or how the technician feels. A sharp tone can affect either person. New evidence may give either person a reason to revise their assessment.

With different equipment, heavier responsibility or a tighter deadline, the experience may differ. Either end can recheck to the process, and this record cannot decide a suffix either.

How to write the two columns: the left records the conclusion, the basis and the confidence at the time; the right records the readings after the recheck, the new evidence, the change in conditions and the change in confidence. Whether or not the conclusions agree, keep the two columns separate; the size of the difference only shows that the judgement then and the material later were different, not the strength of an emotion, and it does not decide how you should assess yourself.

**The type-dynamics convention used here** This page uses Ti–Se–Ni–Fe for ISTP. The Foundation's table allows either attitude for the third process, Intuition. Here Ni means introverted intuition in position three, and Fe means extraverted feeling in position four. The suffix adds no process and has no bearing on skills or behaviour order.

**Editorial fiction statement** The sealing-machine rework and the work order recheck, the lab report sent back, and the conversation in which a partner mentions the leaking tap are all editorial fiction, used only for practice in telling things apart, and correspond to no real work order, report or person.

**Scope limits** This page uses the NERIS definition of Identity for A/T; that definition is not the scoring method of the FermatMind assessment and provides no evidence for its norms. How FermatMind scores and how results are interpreted are set out in the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence). The four-letter sample distribution of MBTI Form M cannot be used to estimate how many people sit at NERIS A/T. Results have to be read together with the setting in which the questions were answered and recent experience, and are not for hiring screening, relationship prediction or ranking ability; health and safety matters follow professional guidance, with clinical judgement resting on a qualified professional.

summary_blocks.body:
ISTP-A and ISTP-T share the four preferences of introversion, sensing, thinking and perceiving. The difference sits in the NERIS Identity used by 16Personalities: A (Assertive) emphasises steadier self-assurance, while T (Turbulent) describes more self-doubt and greater sensitivity to pressure. When a troubleshooting conclusion is rejected, for example, the two ends may do exactly the same checking and still assess themselves differently. The suffix is not one of the four official MBTI preferences, and behaviour cannot decide which end someone sits at.

ISTP stands for Introversion, Sensing, Thinking and Perceiving. These preferences concern attention, concrete information and experience, logical consistency in decisions, and keeping options open in the outer world.

A means Assertive and -T means Turbulent in 16Personalities. The T within ISTP means Thinking. Official MBTI uses four preference pairs. The suffix cannot tell you whose diagnosis is more accurate.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Both are described by ISTP as the same set of preferences, which is the premise of a same-type comparison: attention and energy lean inward, information is gathered with weight on facts and first-hand experience, judgement leans on objective consistent standards, and the outer world tends toward keeping options rather than settling at once. With the same four letters, the behavioural common ground is far larger than the difference.

In 16Personalities' NERIS Identity scale, Assertive describes steadier self-assurance. Turbulent describes greater sensitivity to pressure and a stronger tendency to second-guess yourself. Both people can reach the same assessment of a fault and feel differently about their own work.

In a fictional repair, the same sealing machine returns after servicing. Two technicians can look at the same work order and check the same readings. Afterward, one might still feel confident in the initial assessment while the other wonders whether it missed something. Neither their confidence nor their actions determine whether the machine meets the release requirements.

Actions do not separate the ends. Someone retests on the spot, someone first asks the customer what consumable was changed, and either can appear at either end. What can be reviewed is the self-assessment at that moment: after this diagnosis was overturned, how much confidence remains in your next judgement.

To leave a record that can be looked back on, write down the conclusion, the basis and the confidence at the time; after the recheck write another entry stating which evidence was added, whether the test conditions changed and which way the confidence moved. When the two conclusions disagree, first work out whether more evidence appeared or the conditions changed, and do not infer the emotion at the time from the size of the gap between the two columns.

A recurring experience can help in understanding a test result, but a work order record cannot decide A or T. Whether once or many times, the retesting action and the feeling at the time are not rules for deciding a suffix. The four letters and the function order are on the [ISTP base page](/en/personality/istp), and the definitions of the two terms are in the [NERIS account](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory).

The notation used here is Ti–Se–Ni–Fe for ISTP. The third process is Intuition, written as Ni in this convention. The Myers & Briggs Foundation also lists Ne for that position. Fe is the fourth process. A/T does not change this theoretical order or tell you what someone will do first.
sections.title: ISTP-A and ISTP-T: what they share and where they differ

sections.body_md:
One work order offers five things worth looking at: whether you trust yourself when writing the conclusion, how much confidence in your judgement remains after being contradicted on the spot, how much assurance is left when downtime presses, how you assess your own ability, and how you assess this judgement after the machine goes back.

There is no question of who is more accurate or faster in the table, only of self-assessment. Align three things before reading: whether the same sentence was heard, whether the same responsibility is carried, and whether it is the same work order in hand. A person carrying heavier responsibility naturally feels it more strongly, and it may simply be a different post. In every row the external basis is fixed to the same readings, the same recheck and the same acceptance standard, and all that either end may attend to more is the movement of its own confidence.

The five rows below are five angles chosen by the editors, using one fictional sealing-machine rework to illustrate the two ends of the same Identity dimension:

| The angle observed | ISTP-A (Assertive) | ISTP-T (Turbulent) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Confidence when writing the diagnosis | More inclined to trust that "this inference holds", while still rechecking the same readings | More inclined to suspect "an item was missed", while rechecking the same readings |
| When contradicted on the spot | Hearing the same objection, may still be confident about the other grounds for the inference | Hearing the same objection, may doubt more whether the whole inference holds |
| When downtime presses | May still feel confident in the assessment under time pressure; release depends on the required readings | May feel less certain about the assessment under the same time pressure; release depends on the same readings |
| After finding the same missed point | May see the omission as a specific error and remain confident in their skills | May worry the same error reflects a wider gap in their skills |
| After the machine is returned to the customer | After meeting the same release criteria, may still feel confident about the original assessment | After meeting the same release criteria, may feel less sure of the original assessment |

If an objection raises a safety issue, the same required checks apply regardless of the suffix or how the technician feels. A sharp tone can affect either person. New evidence may give either person a reason to revise their assessment.

sections.body_md:
How the work order should be changed depends on the machine, the spare parts and the customer's conditions; it is borrowed here only to review the self-assessment at the time.

### ISTP-A and ISTP-T face the same rejection

(A fictional scene.) Both are in the repair room, with the same work order, the same machine and the same batch of spare parts.

In this fictional repair, both technicians follow the same verification process and agree on the fault and next step. One might still trust their original reasoning. The other might question whether they overlooked a sign. Both must apply the same release requirements. How confident they feel cannot measure skill or identify an A/T result.

### ISTP-A and ISTP-T at work and in study: the same lab report sent back

(A fictional scene.) The experimental data fall short and the report is returned for rewriting. Both reread the original record, both ask a classmate in the same group, and both revise the wording of the method description.

In the fictional lab example, both students confirm that only the method description needs revising. One may continue to trust their own judgement and another may worry that they will miss a limitation next time. Their reactions cannot identify a suffix or show that either revision is better.

sections.body_md:
Neither reading holds: A does not mean being unable to take advice, and T does not mean being bad at the trade. These two words mark where self-assessment lands, not a score for skill in hand, and they do not measure the quality of a judgement.

To compare who is steadier, do not compare who talks less. Go back to the work order: the original readings, the replacement record, the time of the customer's answer. Who measured what is in the record; that is closer to the facts than who looks more composed.

Another slip is writing the right-hand letter into the code as a fifth letter and reading it as another type. The second letter of ISTP is still S and the third still T; A and T are two ends of one dimension in NERIS Identity, they sit alongside those four rather than composing them, and they are not an official MBTI dimension.

One rework or one retest is not enough to decide a suffix by itself; conversely, a recurring reaction cannot become a decision rule either. On the same work order, either end may retest and either may ask a colleague to check. To compare two results, see the note on retesting in the questions below.
sections.title: ISTP-A and ISTP-T: avoiding misreadings

sections.body_md:
This section does not decide which end you belong to; it only says in which situation one description is closer to your reaction at the time. When the two results are uncertain, do not fight over the label: go back to the work order and write the original judgement and the recheck result in two columns.

When a troubleshooting conclusion is contradicted, note first whether it can be checked against the same readings or records, then record separately whether assurance in the original explanation changed. With different equipment, heavier responsibility or a tighter deadline, the experience may differ. Either end can recheck to the process, and this record cannot decide a suffix either.

How to write the two columns: the left records the conclusion, the basis and the confidence at the time; the right records the readings after the recheck, the new evidence, the change in conditions and the change in confidence. Whether or not the conclusions agree, keep the two columns separate; the size of the difference only shows that the judgement then and the material later were different, not the strength of an emotion, and it does not decide how you should assess yourself.

This record is only for reviewing the self-assessment at the time, not for judging who is better suited to repair work. Whether once or many times, the retesting action and the feeling at the time are not rules for deciding a suffix.
sections.title: ISTP-A and ISTP-T: how to keep observing yourself

items.answer:
The difference lies in Identity within NERIS. It concerns self-assurance, self-assessment and sensitivity to pressure: the A end is usually more confident in its own judgement and less disturbed under pressure; the T end usually doubts more readily and, as pressure rises, finds it harder to trust itself. The behaviour of the two ends can be identical.

With the same sealing machine returned, either end may reopen the work order and retest the stroke; identical actions show no end. What can be seen is whether your assessment of that judgement changed after the work order was closed; a single wavering is not evidence, and even a recurring pattern is only a clue for understanding a test result.
items.question: What is the difference between ISTP-A and ISTP-T?

items.answer:
No. Official MBTI gives only the four letters; A and T are two ends of one dimension in the NERIS Identity of 16Personalities, belonging to another convention. They are not a fifth official MBTI dimension and do not measure the quality of a judgement.

Locate it before reading: the third letter is about the basis of judgement, the right-hand letter about self-assessment and response to pressure; the T after the hyphen is not the T of Thinking. If a report contains no passage explaining that right-hand label, the label should not be counted into the type.
items.question: ISTP-A and ISTP-T: are they two official MBTI kinds of ISTP?

items.answer:
The suffix has nothing to do with it. Repair work needs evidence, tools, authority and experience; either end has people who fix it right first time, and either end has people who struggle with a new model.

In the fictional example, both technicians apply the same acceptance criteria. They can agree on the result while feeling differently about their judgement. Accuracy depends on the evidence and the relevant checks, regardless of how long either person reflects afterward.
items.question: ISTP-A and ISTP-T: who is better at repair work?

items.answer:
The need for rework depends on what was missed and whether the work meets the relevant requirements. Either person may find an omission during the same follow-up. A/T does not predict who will need to redo work.

When reviewing the result, ask what evidence supports the conclusion, whether the test conditions changed and who can confirm the work against the applicable standard. Separate those answers from doubts about your skill.
items.question: ISTP-A and ISTP-T: who is more likely to rework?

items.answer:
Who does the main repair and who rechecks depends on who knows this model, who has the time and who has the signing authority, not on the right-hand letter. Either end has people who can sign off a release, and either has people suited to a second check.

Agree who performs the check, who is authorised to sign off and who updates the customer. Confirm each person has accepted their responsibility. The suffix cannot establish whether that division of work will succeed.
items.question: ISTP-A and ISTP-T: how should two people divide the work on one machine?

items.answer:
In a fictional conversation, a partner says that a tap is leaking again after a repair. You might wonder about the fault or start doubting your ability more broadly. The reaction does not identify an A/T suffix or tell you what caused the leak.

Then state the boundary: which jobs you are willing to take on, and which suggestions should go to a professional. Next time a similar situation arises, discuss it with those two points rather than labelling yourself first.
items.question: ISTP-A and ISTP-T: how do they differ in a relationship?

items.answer:
It is possible. Two different suffixes do not mean the four-letter type changed, and the suffix alone cannot tell you the cause.

First confirm whether it was the same instrument, the same version and the same language; if it was the same measure and the report gives scores, see whether both sit near the dividing line. Then record which stretch of experience each answer referred to and what the circumstances were, as clues for understanding the difference.
items.question: ISTP-A and ISTP-T: I tested as A and later as T; is that normal?

items.answer:
Ask first whether you want the foundation or the detail of one end.

The comparison ends here. The full account of the four letters is on the [ISTP base page](/en/personality/istp); for one end only, go to [ISTP-A](/en/personality/istp-a) or [ISTP-T](/en/personality/istp-t).

**Framework sources** The four letters of official MBTI and type dynamics follow the [Foundation's type dynamics table](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/); the explanation of A/T follows the [16Personalities account of NERIS](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory) and the [Identity page](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/identity-assertive-vs-turbulent).

**The type-dynamics convention used here** This page uses Ti–Se–Ni–Fe for ISTP. The Foundation's table allows either attitude for the third process, Intuition. Here Ni means introverted intuition in position three, and Fe means extraverted feeling in position four. The suffix adds no process and has no bearing on skills or behaviour order.

**Editorial fiction statement** The sealing-machine rework and the work order recheck, the lab report sent back, and the conversation in which a partner mentions the leaking tap are all editorial fiction, used only for practice in telling things apart, and correspond to no real work order, report or person.

**Scope limits** This page uses the NERIS definition of Identity for A/T; that definition is not the scoring method of the FermatMind assessment and provides no evidence for its norms. How FermatMind scores and how results are interpreted are set out in the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence). The four-letter sample distribution of MBTI Form M cannot be used to estimate how many people sit at NERIS A/T. Results have to be read together with the setting in which the questions were answered and recent experience, and are not for hiring screening, relationship prediction or ranking ability; health and safety matters follow professional guidance, with clinical judgement resting on a qualified professional.
